tagline: A climb past power plants into the volcanic Tushar Mountains
intro: Beaver Canyon Scenic Byway climbs 4,000 feet through mountain mahogany and ponderosa pine, passing four hydroelectric plants. The paved road is narrow near the canyon mouth, with enclosed forest views before the hillsides open farther up. It belongs to Utah’s state and National Forest scenic-byway programs. Visit Utah highlights its high-mountain scenery and autumn color on a drive of about 17 miles from Beaver to Eagle Point. The mountains are the remains of a series of volcanoes; Visit Utah dates a period of massive eruptions to about 24 million years ago.

The road east from Beaver to Puffer’s Lake entered the state highway system in 1927 as part of SR-21. In 1941 that route extended across the mountains to Junction; four years later the Beaver–Junction road received its own number, SR-153. Its alignment has changed little since 1945, apart from minor realignments. State scenic-byway recognition followed in 1990, with National Forest recognition in 1991.

From Beaver, 200 North becomes Highway 153 and enters Fishlake National Forest. Beyond the steep climb, Merchant Valley Dam supplies the power plants below, and the road levels into alpine meadows. Continue past the ski-area development to the end of pavement near Puffer Lake. The road beyond belongs to the Kimberly/Big John Scenic Backway and is unpaved.
notice: Mountain mahogany and ponderosa pine line the climb past four hydroelectric plants.

moments.title: Beaver
moments.text: Beaver’s river supplied an early hydroelectric plant that continues to provide a large share of the town’s power. The river comes out of the Tushar Mountains and passes south of downtown before flowing west toward Minersville. The town’s earlier growth followed another transport corridor: Mormon settlers arrived along the Mormon Road in 1856. That wagon route linked settlements spaced a day’s horseback ride apart. The mountain drive begins on 200 North, which becomes Highway 153 east of downtown. It starts at Main Street, where SR-153 meets SR-160, before following the canyon into Fishlake National Forest.

moments.title: Merchant Valley Dam
moments.text: Merchant Valley Dam supplies water to the power plants lower in Beaver Canyon. Visit Utah places it three miles beyond Mahogany Cove, after the steep climb through forested hillsides. Above the dam, the road levels across flat alpine meadowland crossed by ATV trails. The surrounding Tushars are the remains of volcanoes, with Mount Baldy, Mount Belknap and Delano Peak all exceeding 12,000 feet. Farther along the road, the signed Big John Flat turnoff leads toward the old Kimberly mining district. Visit Utah records log ruins and the remains of the Annie Laurie mill in that mining district.
moments.notice: Above the dam, forested slopes give way to flat alpine meadowland crossed by ATV trails.

moments.title: Puffer Lake
moments.text: Near Puffer Lake, the pavement ends and Highway 153 continues as a dirt road across the Tushars. The highway reaches a paved elevation of 9,200 feet in this area, then climbs higher after the surface changes. Visit Utah identifies the continuation as part of the Kimberly/Big John Scenic Backway. Its first unpaved stretch is steep and narrow; farther east, switchbacks descend toward the Sevier River Valley. That continuation is closed in winter. Visit Utah describes the onward trip as impractical for RVs and trailers because of the narrow climb and switchbacks.

practical: Puffer Lake: Visit Utah states that snow tires or chains are required in Beaver Canyon November 1–March 31. The unpaved road east of Puffer Lake closes in winter; check its status in Beaver before continuing. (checked 2026-10-11)
